segments.expected: She had decided at noon, sitting on the edge of her bed with her book on her knee. She had read Hart's second card again, which she kept between the last page and the cover. What do the two fingers tell you through iron? Try it properly, and write down how it comes out, whichever way. She had tried it properly. She had tried it on her aunt's surface plate and in her aunt's vice, on a free Saturday in the twelfth month, forty-nine times, and written down every one. Six in seven. She had never written back to him with the answer. She had meant to. It had seemed better said than written.

The street went down a ramp from the quay, and then it was level. The houses on either side were small and close and neat, with their doors painted, and their steps whitened, and boxes of something green in the windows. And behind the houses on the right, where the harbour was, there was a wall.

segments.expected: She had a question. She had had it since the autumn, since the night at Ferren with a keeper's book under a desk lamp, and a line in brown ink that she had read twice. Somebody at Saltmere had a temperature as well. This man had known what the bank was before anybody told him. He had known it with the bad hand. He had sat in this pump house at twenty past two on the seventeenth of the ninth month, and she wanted to know, very badly, whether he had been hot that night, and whether he had slept, and what he had seen if he had.

segments.expected: "There's a Board warrant," she said. "We came south on it. The Company's stretched to the last man with the springs coming on, and four tears on the Longshore this week, and the Board's sent for vans from inland to stand on Company ground under Company eyes." She took a slate out of her pocket and did not look at it. "I've two nights left on your card. If the Company calls us on Monday, it'll be one of them. Pike rides as a voice. They'll lend us a catcher. You're Pike's second, as before."

segments.expected: There was a thing she could have said then. It was short, and true, and it would have cost her something. She knew what it was. She had known for twenty years. She did not say it. She stood there until the light was gone off the water, and he did not turn round, and at last she went back along the walk, a step at a time, the way she had come.
